subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-OPPORTUNITY FOR DISCUSSION
speechtext:

Canada is active in negotiations with a number of countries, and if it does not seem that progress is being made I can only say the fault for that lack of progress in bringing about a cease fire does not at this moment rest entirely on the United States. There are other countries which are showing a reluctance to bring about a cease fire or to recognize conditions which would make a cease fire possible. Canada, with the United Kingdom and others, is engaged in a process of discussion which does not in any circumstances warrant the suggestion that we are not doing everything we can in respect of a situation in which we are not the primary agent. The other day in the British house a request was made for a debate. The attitude taken there by the British prime minister is
Inquiries of the Ministry not unlike the attitude which I am taking at this moment, and I am sure the right hon. gentleman will agree that Britain has a responsibility in this matter certainly not less than that of a country such as Canada.

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-OPPORTUNITY FOR DISCUSSION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: TAKING OF YOUNG SEALS BY LAND BASED OPERATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. It is an aftermath of his announcement of the decision of the government not to increase the quota of baby seals to be taken this year beyond the 50,000 figure. With this decision I am in complete agreement. My question is, has the minister any information as to the possibility that remaining baby seals are in danger of being carried by the ice floes so close to the mainland that they become exposed to land based operations, resulting in their being taken in quantities greatly exceeding the maximum allowed quota?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minisler of Fisheries):
subtopic: TAKING OF YOUNG SEALS BY LAND BASED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall, as stated by the hon. member who has just asked the question, that last Thursday I announced, and confirmed again yesterday, that the quota established for the catch of young harp seals less than one year old in gulf area 2 would be reached that day, and no additional young seals would be taken there by licensed sealers after that date. I understand many hon. members, including myself, are receiving a large number of telegrams which read something like this: "Urge no increased quota on sealing" or "We protest increased quota on seal skins", and others to that effect.
In order to clear up any possible misunderstanding concerning the application of the quota I wish to point out that the quota applies only to licensed seal fishermen operating from licensed vessels and aircraft. The catch of young seals by landsmen who are able to take seals when the ice comes close to shore is not included in the quota. I want to add

that this was understood by members of the industry and officials of the S.P.C.A. and other humane societies, who met with us in Moncton and Ottawa last year before the regulations were amended.
This catch by landsmen is of importance to local communities along the shores of the gulf of St. Lawrence, and the fishermen use small boats less than 30 feet in length to carry out their fishing operations. The number of young seals taken by landsmen was taken into full consideration when the quota for licensed sealers was established, and experience shows that the landsmen's catch does not now constitute a serious threat to conservation of the harp seal stocks in the area.
The favourable conditions which prevailed during the first few days of the fishing season this year would have led to a large catch of young seals if the quota had not been in effect. It would have been possible for the licensed sealers to catch a very high percentage of the young seals born this year, and this would have caused a serious reduction in the harp seal population of the gulf.
For the information of hon. members I should like to say that an additional conservation measure included in the seal protection regulations for this year prohibits the killing of mature seals in the breeding patches. This regulation protects the mature breeding females which constitute the most important segment of the population. Juveniles and adult males which congregate outside the breeding patches may be taken throughout the fishing season which closes on April 25 in the gulf area. The sealers use large calibre rifles to kill these animals.
It is expected that there will be a sharp reduction in commercial sealing activities in the gulf area now that the quota of young seals has been taken, but the department's officers will continue their patrols to ensure that the regulations are adhered to by those who continue to hunt the older seals.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS REQUEST RESPECTING WHITE RUSSIAN REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last, March 12, the hon. member for Marquette inquired whether the Canadian government had received a request from the United Nations' high commissioner for refugees concerning the possible admission of 200 white Russians to Canada. The hon. member also asked that I explain in the event that it developed that the department had refused any such request.
I have looked into the matter, Mr. Speaker, and I find that no direct representations have in fact been made by the high commissioner, although in August, 1964 representatives of this group of white Russians in Hong Kong wrote directly to several immigration offices in Canada as well as to our office in Hong Kong regarding this matter.

Inquiries of the Ministry
By way of explanation, I might add that in the past several years my department has received representations from the Tolstoy Foundation and other bodies on behalf of groups of people in several parts of the world who are described as "old believers". These inquiries have come not only from the Far East but from Turkey, Brazil and the United States. Briefly, the "old believers" are a religious sect, who wish to migrate to a country where they will be able to follow their customary way of life in a community separate and distinct from the general population. In the Tolstoy Foundation's own words, these people are "intellectually very primitive, with small knowledge of world events or politics".
From the department's experience over the years-and I might say that the department's views in this regard are shared by a great many of my colleagues from British Columbia and western Canada generally-it has been found that group settlements such as these are undesirable and they often create special problems. It is unlikely that such people would be able to overcome the many difficulties which they would have to face if they came to Canada as a group.
In the circumstances, therefore, it has been necessary to advise these persons from whom letters have been received that we cannot in principle accept group movements. We did say, however, that if individual applications were received each individual application would be studied on its merits.

Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec: and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses: and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
I read the whole section so it would be on the record, but obviously the part which is germane is the middle part, where it says:
-and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses-
I realize that if we were a court of law we would be required to have a pretty thorough inquiry into the definition of words such as "records" and "journals" and decide what they mean, especially when those words begin with capital letters. But taking those words in their ordinary meaning it would seem to me that the minutes of proceedings and evidence of a committee of this house-and
Canada Pension Plan
we must remember that by our standing orders all house committees are regarded as extensions of the house-should be printed in both languages. In other words, I think the standing orders of the house do not, perhaps, go as far as they should go in the light of the requirements of the British North America Act.
There have been many arguments on this language question about how far bilingualism should be carried, but there is no question but that the two languages are equal in the parliament of Canada. There may be a question about it somewhere else, but there is no question here. So I believe the hon. member for Beauce has a valid point of privilege, and in discussing this point of privilege we should start from that point. We should start with a clear recognition of the validity of the point.

I have been interested in this question for some time, and I have made some inquiries in some of the offices about the building. I have found that it has always been the practice to translate all the minutes of proceedings, though they may have been taken in English, into French. That has always been the case for all our committees; but the tendency over the years has been to do this five or six months after the event in periods between sessions of parliament. That was not good enough but it has been the practice.

It is also true that several new translators were hired. I recognize that there is a recruiting problem, which I think is due to the fact that the salary offered is lower than that offered by private industry in Montreal, Quebec or elsewhere.

The recommendations of the committee were, in the main, of a technical nature and of minor consequence. The amendments put forward by the opposition fall into the same class. There is now some misgiving as to the likely operation of the plan in its original form by the beginning of next year.
The plan was initially introduced as a social measure being part of the platform of the Liberal party. When it was revised in view of a consolidation, this involved a supplementary source of capital for the federal and provincial governments.

The question of privilege is valid because the two languages are recognized as official languages of parliament. It has been our understanding all these years that all reports would be printed in both languages. Time and again I recall, when I sat on the other side of the house, that when reports were tabled questions were asked as to whether they were printed in both languages. If the reports had not been translated into the other language, then objection was very properly raised.
It has been the custom over the years to have the report of committee meetings translated into both languages. As one of my colleagues pointed out, time and again members of this house whose native language is French have been very generous in letting us proceed in committee on other occasions when the document in front of us was printed in only one language, namely English. They have been exceptionally generous along that line. During the last few years the problem has been recognized in this house, and thanks to the action taken by the Progressive Conservative government simultaneous translation was provided in this chamber and has made it much more effective. For the first time in

many years interested members may use the translation system to follow debates in either language. At the same time, I well recall that we had difficulty in getting sufficient translators to maintain the volume of work which faced us in getting reports and other documents translated. Many times we fell behind and there were delays. But the problem has come increasingly to the fore.
The problem of finding suitable translators is recognized on both sides of the house, but it is high time that a major effort is made which is even greater than that which has been up to the present so as to ensure that translation shall be rapid, accurate and complete. We have achieved that with regard to Hansard and are able to receive our copies in either language the following day. I also think it has been fairly well achieved with regard to departmental reports, although I have not recently checked to make sure.
I was under the impression that we had achieved success with regard to committee work, although there there is a delay both in the finalizing of the English version as well as the French. That is another problem which should be settled before too long, because there is too much delay in the presentation of committee reports.
However, the house has expressed its astonishment today at finding that the pension committee report has not been translated and made available to those members of this house who want it in the French language. I did not know until today that this circumstance prevailed. Surely this is a valid question of privilege. There are two recognized official languages. Members of this house are right to insist that they should have put before them the documents of this house in their own language. I would be one of the first to object, I think, if documents were put before me in one language when I wanted them in the other. I read more freely in the English language than I do in the French, although I read both; but I would be one of the first to insist that documents be put before me in the English language.
In this particular matter, dealing with a joint pension committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, it is incredible that provision was not made for the translation of the evidence presented before that committee. As I mentioned earlier this afternoon, the joint committee met during a recess of parliament and it would seem normal that the translators who work here from day to day would have been available for that com-
Question of Privilege
mittee work. I do not know of any other committee that was sitting during the recess.
We are prepared to grant that the job is a large one, that it requires highly skilled workers and that there are sometimes inevitable delays. I doubt very much that anyone would have objected had there been a delay of a week or two in the production of the French version of the committee reports, but much more time than that has gone by. The proceedings of the committee covering work it performed in the months of January and February apparently have not yet been translated into the French language.
So, Mr. Speaker, the objection raised by the hon. member for Beauce, with whose party I am seldom in agreement, is on this occasion a valid objection and should be sustained by the House of Commons because a principle is involved here. If we have two languages they must have equal standing in parliament. It is not right to relegate one of those languages to a secondary position, which is what has been done on this occasion. After all the years of experience I would have thought that great care would be taken to give proper recognition to the French language. So I support the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Beauce. It is valid and in my opinion it should be considered to be valid by the Chair.

After all, this session is still in existence, because the government promised long ago that it would not be prorogued until this important piece of legislation was finally passed. This assurance was confirmed yesterday by the Prime Minister.
Question of Privilege
We do not need to go over some of the things which were dealt with earlier in committee of the whole but I would remind the house of the fact that standing order 74 goes part of the way into this problem by requiring that all bills be presented in both languages. I would remind the house also that the British North America Act, which is even more demanding than the standing orders governing this house, requires-and I am reading the middle portion of section 133-that both languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of this house. When I spoke earlier I suggested there might be some argument over definitions-argument as to what is meant by records and journals. I think it was on that point that the ruling was made to which the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) alluded a while ago. But may I point out-and this just emphasizes how serious the problem is; this just emphasizes the fact that we have got to cope with it-that I think on all sides of the house, and I include my friends at the far end of the house who have raised this issue, we can be reasonable people and resolve it.

The minutes of proceedings and evidence accompanying the said report recorded as appendix No. 23 to the Journals.

Now, Mr. Speaker, whether it is a question of privilege or a point of order is a good question. For the most part the President of the Privy Council and the Minister of Labour addressed themselves to this question and argued that it was not a proper question of privilege because it had not been raised soon enough; and I can see the possibility that this might be Your Honour's ruling. But even they admit that if it is not a question of privilege it could be, and probably is, a point of procedure. In this regard I say to my friends to the far left-that "far left" is geographically, not politically-that privilege in this case is a word that we apply to something a person has a right to raise in the house. I am not denying that the use of the French language is just as much a privilege or right as is the use of the English language in the federal parliament of this country. But even if it is decided that it is not a question of privilege, surely it is a point of order and surely it is a point of procedure when we read in the Journals of the House of Commons of February 16, in both languages, that issues Nos. 1 to 24 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence were tabled.
I say, as I said when I was dealing with this same issue an hour or two ago when we were in committee of the whole, that I think we should all recognize the magnitude of this problem of translation. We should recognize the way it has grown, in an explosive fashion, in the last few years. I think tribute should be paid to the staff and to those who have stepped up the speed with which things

have been translated. But we have not yet outgrown the practice of a few years ago which seemed to involve committee minutes being translated into French six months later. That apparently was the practice for many years. Progress has been made. Just as I would ask that the house recognize the validity of the point being made by our friends in the far corner, I hope our friends in the far corner will recognize that progress has been made in this regard and that they might be willing, if Your Honour takes this whole question under advisement, to meet in a conference of representatives of the government and the other parties and see if there is not some way that we can resolve this issue.
We do not want, as a parliament of Canada, to say anything that downgrades the use of or the right to use either language in this House of Commons. But it is also true that a parliament that has spent nearly two years on the Canada pension plan does not want to see it shelved; does not want to see it delayed. I think that by a conference of reasonable people representing all parties of this house we could reach a resolution of this question. I hope there will not be attempts to exacerbate the situation. I hope it will be accepted for its seriousness. I support very strongly the suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), and I think the Minister of Labour supported it, too. His only qualification was that we should have some argument first- and we are having it. But I hope Your Honour will take the matter under advisement and that somebody from the government side, the President of the Privy Council, the acting prime minister or someone else, might consider the suggestion of calling a conference of people representing all parties in this house to see if we cannot resolve in an amicable and reasonable way this very important issue.

The Minister of Labour stated that if we waited for the committee proceedings to be translated into French, we could not adopt the pension plan this session. That is an argument made by the Minister of Labour.
But the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned that standing order 74 of the House of Commons reads as follows:
All bills shall be printed before the second reading in the English and French languages.
Before.
I also consider it from that point of view as regards all that is related to this bill or to any other bill. However, the responsibility to make a ruling lies with you.
Here is citation 119 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms on which I should like to put some emphasis. A while ago I quoted paragraph 2 of this citation and now I should like to quote paragraphs 1 and 2 together and read them to you carefully, precisely to present opposition to the opinion put forward by the Minister of Labour and by the President of the Privy Council a while ago. Here is what is said in paragraph 1 of citation 119:
One of the main functions of the house consists in debating public issues, a function which can only be filled by complete freedom of speech.
As I understand this sentence, it means that before one can exercise complete freedom of speech, one must have all the documents required to take part in the debate.
Later on, it says:
There will always be contests between groups and parties, minority and majority, and in the debates that follow, the rules of procedure are all important.
We now have to deal with a rule of procedure, namely the one set out by the Minister of Labour and by the President of the Privy Council, that is whether there is a valid question of privilege in view of the time when it was raised.
I go on reading the citation:
Delays, multiplicity of amendments and even obstruction must not always be regarded as illegitimate political weapons. Rules of absolute rigidity have no place in the House of Commons. The United Kingdom house has gone further than us in modernizing some of its rules. Although we may take a leaf out of its book, we have developed a parliamentary practice of our own based on British principles and yet clearly Canadian. While we appreciate the long experience of the United Kingdom house and seek to profit therefrom-
The last sentence is very important under the present circumstances, because the point
Question of Privilege
at issue here is not only a matter of translation but also a matter of principle, of right, of prerogatives.
Here is the last sentence of this paragraph 1 of citation 119.
-we are the absolute and independent masters of our own procedure in accordance with our circumstances and needs.
Consequently, we are responsible for finding a solution without stumbling over one hundred and one procedures. We are never 100 per cent bound to a procedure or a precedent established in this house; it is our responsibility to make an immediate decision in accordance with the circumstances.
I do not agree with the Minister of Labour when he says that there is no question of privilege, because it was not raised one or two weeks ago. An injustice is always an injustice, whether it happens today or took place two weeks ago. That is no reason to tell us that we have to put up with that injustice now.
I will now read paragraph (2) of citation 119 which in fact contradicts the minister's argument that this would prolong the session and prevent the adoption of the pension plan:
The mere object of shortening sessions may lead to an undue curtailment of the freedom of speech. The duties of a representative parliament are too important to be performed in a hurry. No question should be decided until it has been fully discussed.
Therefore, the question should be fully discussed. We need the reports of the special joint committee which considered Bill No. C-136, the most complex piece of legislation which has ever been submitted to the Canadian parliament in 20 years.
Although some effort ought to be made to economize time, every shade of opinion has the right to find expression and members who desire to give their views should not be prevented from doing so. Canada is a vast country, extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific ocean. The problems of the west are not those of the east. The viewpoints of members of parliament from British Columbia and the prairie provinces differ from those of Ontario:	Ontario differs from
Quebec-
And we, in this group, are a part of Quebec.

And referring to the matter under discussion, that is restriction of the debate, if we only had the necessary information, the translation of the joint committee reports on Bill No. C-136.

And today, a great many rules have been referred to in trying to tell the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Perron) you have no right. It is not up to you to deal with this question of privilege. We feel we would be discriminated against today if we do not obtain translation of the proceedings of the committee which considered Bill No. C-136.
Freedom of speech is a sacred principle-
Here, as elsewhere, and not only for the public at large. It is all very well to put on a show for the public at large. But let us put it into practice in the House of Commons. Let us practise what we preach, which will make it that much easier to respect freedom.
-and if there is a place where it should be fully respected that place is the parliament of the nation, and it is the Speaker's responsibility-
I am speaking to Your Honour at present-

Mr. Speaker, I want to submit one or two points for your consideration. The first is that the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), in what I choose to classify as a specious argument that privilege must be raised at the first opportunity, conveniently overlooked the fact that it was only this afternoon that we returned to clause 1 of this bill. This method for the consideration of bills is one of the reforms made by the procedure committee which was recommended to and accepted by the house.
I submit that the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Perron) exercised the utmost courtesy and consideration. He did not invoke his privilege until clause 1 was reached. He made a helpful and co-operative attempt to give time to the translation staff and to the government to do what it is constitutionally bound to do, that is, to provide records in both official languages.
I submit that the hon. member for Beauce, who raised this question of privilege, would be guilty of neglect and would fail in his responsibility to his constituents and to those millions of Canadians whose working language is French if he had not raised this question of privilege. It is not good enough, Mr. Speaker, merely to pay lip service to the constitution of the country. We are here as guardians and protectors of the constitution. Section 133 of the British North America Act, an entrenched section if I ever saw one, makes it mandatory, not permissive but mandatory, that the records and journals be in both languages.
I am going to suggest, as has been suggested by other hon. members, that the report of the committee which considered the Canada pension plan is very much a part of the records of the house. But even if I fail on this argument the report has become, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), part of the Journals and the same mandatory injunction

applies that the material be available in both languages. For your consideration, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote at this point citation 288 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, found on page 237:
Committees are regarded as portions of the house and are governed for the most part in their proceedings by the same rules which prevail in the house.
This is just one other part of a foundation which I think has been built by those hon. members who feel there is a valid question of privilege here. I suggest, in fact I ask the question: Is it not extraordinarily ironical that a government which sets in motion a royal commission on bilingualism and bicul-turalism should now seek to take refuge behind frivolous and quibbling points of order? They are taking such refuge when a genuine and constitutionally guaranteed right of bilingualism, not just a royal commission, is being challenged.
The Minister of Labour sought to supply you, Mr. Speaker, and us with an oversize red herring in his threat that we must pass the bill or else the session will end without its passage. As most of us know, red herrings are the business of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud), not of the Minister of Labour.
Under what law or custom does the minister base his charge that the session will end? Who says so? Certainly not the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in his answer of the other day. The throne speech, Mr. Speaker, contains an as yet untapped mine of Liberal promises which the government could bring forward. We would be delighted to consider them. Your research, Mr. Speaker, may lead you to the conclusion, as a matter of fact, that the entire discussion of the bill may have been irregular and that the government will be forced to submit an ex post facto order regularizing what has been done up to now.
I have one final word, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested a reasonable approach and because we are reasonable people we can agree with him. But added to a reasonable approach I suggest that the government indulge in a crash translation program. I suggest that the government make a real and genuine effort. I suggest that the government seek volunteers from the universities in this capital city to do this job as evidence of their earnest in the duality of this country. I even suggest that the government take steps which will "excite the daring", to use words which have become rusty
Question of Privilege
from disuse. I suggest that the government not run for cover behind irrelevant precedents and points of order which beg the fundamental principle involved.
Mr. H, A. Olson (Medicine Hat):	Mr. Speaker, I think the argument advanced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) earlier today that this question of privilege could not be raised at this time because it was not the first or earliest opportunity to do so is a very poor argument. Furthermore, I think that the veiled threat of the minister, although I know he tried to clarify his words, that it would be impossible to get the bill through at this session of parliament if the question of privilege were accepted is also a rather poor way of attempting to defeat the motion based on the question of privilege.
On the other hand, I am very much concerned about the precedent we may set if we accept as a question of privilege the fact that the evidence of any committee is not before parliament at the time of proceeding with a bill or motion based upon the work of that committee. There are many instances in the past where the house has dealt with a bill or motion which had been considered by a standing committee of the house, and has done so long before the evidence of the committee was printed in either English or French.
We have standing committees of the house meeting right at the present time. For example, the committee on agriculture and colonization, the committee on privileges and elections and the committee on mines, forests and waters are all meeting. If this question of privilege is accepted, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that none of the reports from any of these committees could be debated in the house and the motions or bills in connection therewith could not be dealt with unless all of the evidence was before us in both languages. In my view it is quite impossible for that to take place if we are going to finish this session within a reasonable length of time.

bill or motion has gone through this House of Commons.
There is one very serious problem in connection with this particular instance, and that is the one the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised this afternoon when he pointed to page 1039 of Votes and Proceedings for Tuesday, February 16. Paragraph 11 reads as follows:
A copy of the committee's Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence (issues Nos. 1 to 24), respecting Bill C-136, is appended.
I presume when that was tabled it did become part ef the Journals of this house. Of course, I do not dispute that any document which is part of the Journals of this house must be printed in both languages. I think, Mr. Speaker, that we ought to be a little reasonable about this matter and perhaps here is where the mistake was made. Perhaps the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence should not have been tabled as an appendix to the report. Certainly the report was available in both languages when it was tabled. The bill was available in both languages during its progress through this house, as were all the amendments. So, Mr. Speaker, I hope you will take this into consideration.
I should like to ask Your Honour also to check and ascertain whether or not the evidence that was in fact tabled on February 16 was printed in the language in which it was spoken. If he did, then I suggest that this complies with the requirements of the section which say the documents shall be in both languages.
I am very concerned that if this question of privilege is accepted as a valid one, we are going to seriously impair the progress of this house in so far as reports and bills coming back from standing committees are concerned. It would be setting a precedent that would allow any member to raise a question of privilege and prevent any further progress with a bill or motion unless all the evidence were printed in both languages and available to the members. I should like however to take exception to the argument put forward by the Minister of Labour today. He said that because this question was not raised on the first day the house dealt with this question, it was no longer a question of privilege. Most of the members of this house read English and a number read French. Some of us are fortunate enough to be able to read both languages. The fact still remains that there are some who cannot read the English language and many who cannot read the French language. So long as both of these languages are the legal languages of this house, as they have always been since the founding of this country, I believe that on a matter as important as this in relation to a bill that is going to affect each and every person across this country, we have a very definite question of privilege each and every minute this debate is carried on when that evidence is not available to all hon. members.

I feel this is very definitely a question of privilege and some action should be taken before debate on this bill is completed.

Mr. Speaker, there are one or two points which should be added to what has been said already in this argument, although it is with some trepidation that I creep into the debate having in mind what has just taken place. Let me first rebut three propositions that have been made from the government side to suggest that there is no valid point of privilege to be considered by Your Honour. These consist of the statements made by the President of the Privy Council, the Minister of Labour and the Secretary of State.
It has been stated, first, that the point taken is not a valid one because it was not taken advantage of at the first suitable opportunity. In reply to that, Your Honour, may I point out that this is a continuing breach of privilege. Every minute this debate continues without the French translation of the evidence before the committee being filed, there continues to be a breach of privilege. If we were to adopt the very useful suggestion made by my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), which Your Honour thought there might be permission of the house to do, I point out that if I were to agree I would be condoning the breach of privilege which we maintain does exist and which Your Honour has not yet decided. If you do so decide, we would then be compounding the offence. I think there is no answer to that and I suggest this point must be decided before we can continue with this
[Mr. GregoireJ
debate. Every minute we debate any particular aspect of this bill without the French translation of these proceedings being filed constitutes a breach of privilege. I think that we can take advantage of it at any time.
The Minister of Labour suggested that if this had to be done the bill might not be passed because the session would conclude. I take this to be a roundabout means of suggesting that our insistence upon this point means interference with the government's timetable for the new session of parliament. This may be very unfortunate and I would hate to be inconveniencing the government. I know how much they look forward to this new session. However, I think something must give, either the government's plans or the pension bill. This is something upon which the government must make a choice. If we are correct in this assumption and this point of privilege does exist, then the government will have to find some way out of the difficulty which they have caused.
So far as the Secretary of State was concerned I judged the text of his remarks constituted an admission that the government was in the wrong and he was simply asking that the sentence be commuted. I think if the government would admit it was wrong and throw itself on the mercy of a compassionate and reasonable opposition we would probably give this assistance to them.
Let me make this point, Your Honour. This is not only a breach of privilege but an especially serious breach of privilege in that it constitutes a denial of a mandatory requirement in the B.N.A. Act under section 133, which has been referred to by several hon. members-and it might be wise at this stage to remind the house of the effect of it. If what we see as the meaning of that section is correct, then the continuation of this debate without the French proceedings being filed is completely erroneous and unconstitutional.
Section 133 is the famous section in respect of which the French language is made official with regard to certain proceedings. It states: Either the English or the French language- And I call attention to the word either, -may he used by any person in the debates of the houses of parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used-
I call attention to the word shall.
-in the respective records and journals of those houses;
Then it repeats the word either.
-and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada-

Surely the distinction made between the use of the word "may" in two instances and the word "shall" can result in no other interpretation than a peremptory command laid on this house that its proceedings shall be in both languages and the records of its proceedings shall be in both languages.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and my hon. friend from Royal made it quite plain that these committee proceedings have been introduced into the Journals of the house. In addition, the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) pointed to the citation from Beauchesne that any committee of the house is an extension of the house and that the same rules, so far as may be possible, shall be related to the committees as are used in the house.
I think it is very simple to find a reason for that. Here we are discussing a complex, complicated and difficult bill which constitutes a complete innovation in our system of social justice. The government saw fit, and quite properly, following suggestions from the opposition, to refer this bill to a committee so that there could be in that committee direct confrontation between members of the committee and witnesses called to explain the terms of this very contentious measure.
Now, coming to the debate in the committee of the whole and the consideration clause by clause, I submit it is a condition precedent to an intelligent and reasonable discussion of the bill that each member of the house should have available for his examination, in the language which he sees fit to use, a complete verbatim record of the proceedings before the special committee. How is this possible, having in mind the failure to file the transcript in the French language? It is quite obvious that there cannot and could not be a fair and reasonable debate for this reason.
Just in the event that Your Honour has not yet come to a decision, although I am sure you probably have, that it is a valid point of privilege, I ask you to bear these facts in mind because it is not only this case which is involved. This case may constitute a precedent. If I do not want my colleagues to embark on a debate before the proceedings are filed in the French language, equally I do not feel I should be compelled to participate in a debate until proceedings were filed in the English language. I suggest this is a matter to be decided not only on the basis of this bill but on the effect it will have in future debates and proceedings in the house.

Mr. Speaker, over the past few months I have

wondered why the Liberal party are getting themselves into so much trouble, and so easily. I am surprised that today we find them getting into exactly the same position. We have heard a lot of impassioned speeches about the fact that Canada has two official languages and that the proceedings in committees and in the house shall be in the two official languages.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) was pleased to stand up and say on behalf of the Liberal party and the government of the day that certain improvements have been made in this regard. Improvements have been made in the last few years, but that was not necessarily because of the political parties which formed the governments of the day. The translation system which we have was brought in during the last few years and I think it has done a great deal to solve the problems with which the country was faced.
We have heard the legal arguments. We have just heard the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), who is well versed in the law, outline the law. Also this afternoon we listened to a threat being made by a cabinet minister that the pension plan could not be passed unless the opposition were to give way. I think it would be fair to say there are one or two members on the government benches who feel that the two official languages are important to this country. But I do not know if there are more than two who have the guts to stand up and vote that way, because they have more interest in being re-elected under a particular banner than they sometimes have in being honest. If there is a vote, we will know how many of them are honest, how many really believe in their French culture and French tongue, how many really believe they should have the right to discuss important business like the pension plan in their own language.
They will have to make this decision because the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) has said it is going to take six weeks to have this translated, or four weeks, or possibly two weeks. I ask how many members of the house remember that the special joint committee first sat on November 24? The seventh report of proceedings before it, which has been filed in French, was dated December 9.
During the recess period there were no translators being used in the house. There were no translators being used in any of the committees while this committee was meeting. I tell you this government is completely incompetent. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pear-

son), who sat in this house a while ago, and who I thought was going to say he believed in the principle that he has talked about- though in many other ways he is quite willing to give Canada away to the provinces- apparently was not willing to argue on a basic principle of having two cultures and two languages.
It seems to me we are being handed a line of malarkey when we are told an effort is being made. The Secretary of State says they are training new people and are providing a school in Montreal. He says there are translation services there. But, Mr. Speaker, there is no translation for me in my office. I ask the French Canadians here: Are they interested in knowing the reasons why this was not translated? I do not speak French, but I was shocked at the beginning of this session when it was pointed out that Beau-chesne, for example, had not been translated into the French language. I did not know that. No one had protested about it before. It seems to me there is no excuse for what has happened. It is all very well for the Minister of Labour to say we shall not do it because it would take too long. I have a few observations to make on the question of privilege which the house has now been considering for some time.
It seems to me we have gone far away from the facts of our present situation. It is easy for me to recognize the righteous in-
Question of Privilege
dignation of the hon. member for Beauce when he finds he cannot have available to him a written transcript of the evidence heard by the committee. He makes this indignation plain in the house. I am sure he is aware that since 1934 the Translation Bureau Act passed by this house has centred in the bureau of translations all the responsibility to interpret language for all bureaux, branches, commissions, and agencies created or appointed by act of parliament or by order of the governor in council in the making and revising of translations from one language into another of all departmental and other reports, documents, debates, bills, acts, proceedings and correspondence.
I draw this to your attention on the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. A practice has grown up under which the English version of the committee reports has been printed, and not until it has been printed has the translation taken place. Therefore a delay occurs before the French version of the committee proceedings comes before the House of Commons. Together with this another practice grew up which was condoned over the years, under which the house received the report of the committee in both languages and the bill, of course, in both languages, but more often than not the French language version of the committee proceedings was not available for consideration by the members of this house. On the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I think that the practice which grew up and was sustained was wrong, and I believe that practice should be changed.
In my opinion this is the question to which we should address ourselves. The question of privilege should result in an expression of a grievance, really; the inability of a member of the house to interpret from another language the finer meanings of an intricate piece of legislation. But, Mr. Speaker, I think the action to be taken now should be constructive. I do not think it should be sufficient for us to decide only a question of privilege. The more important thing is, what can we do to correct this disability from which the French speaking members in this house suffer? That is the important question.
The important thing, then, is to recognize that the question of privilege really is a complaint against a practice which has prevailed in this house and should no longer continue. It is my opinion that there is a practical solution. We should not hold up current legislation that is before the house because of this improper or unfair practice. I think a resolution should be put before the house by the

Question of Privilege
gentleman who has raised the question of privilege that this inadequacy on the part of our house staff to submit promptly to us both the French and English versions of committee proceedings should be a matter to be sent to the privileges and elections committee.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I would say that it seems to me, from what has been said here tonight, that there has been far more heat than light. If we examine this question from the point of view of fundamental principles, there is only one principle against which we must check our decision and thinking, and that is the rights of French Canadians in this country under the constitution. These were spelled out in 1867 when the constitution provided that reports shall be in two languages. Therefore anyone, any government which tries to hide behind statements, such as we have heard tonight from the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd) and others on the government side are simply trying to cover up what they should have known at the beginning, namely that these reports and proceedings should be provided in two languages. They should have preserved the constitution. If they believed what they have been saying, they should have had these reports and proceedings presented to this house in two languages.
The Secretary of State said that certain schools are in operation for the training of translators in order that people may receive more training and more translators will be available. But what has this to do with not bringing in these reports and proceedings in both languages, which the constitution requires? It does not answer the question. If the Secretary of State really wanted to be efficient, and if the government wanted to be efficient, these proceedings were translated simultaneously in the committee and they could have been recorded on tape and typed out afterwards, if they did not have anybody there to write them out. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to put forward these excuses is weakening the government's argument and is showing clearly that this failure was because of inefficiency.
May I say that the Minister of Labour also made the statement that it would take two weeks, or three weeks, or a month, or three

months to translate these proceedings, and this would hold up the passing of the legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I asked today of the minister was asked previously in the session by the


hon. member for Peace River, I think it was, and the hon. member for Edmonton West. It concerns what has been called by the Edmonton Journal something that is "big, bold and iffy". The reason I raise the question is because my interest in railway matters has caused me to receive many communications from people in Alberta who feel that this project of building a railway through the formation of a provincial crown corporation-the whole thing should be built and maintained and managed by the Canadian National Railways-is nothing more than a ploy to fit in with a particular by-election campaign at the present time.
It might be useful to hear what Premier Manning did say about this. Incidentally, he made his speech, which touched on the details of this matter, in February, and despite the fact that most of the bills before the Alberta legislature this session are now available in the library of parliament, there is still no bill available on this particular matter. The premier did say that the line was not going to go ahead unless commitments of some kind were received from industry. It is quite apparent that the plan is for the line to be hooked up with the C.N.R. line, to move north from the C.N.R. line and eventually to link up with the C.N.R. line several hundred miles farther north. In other words, it would be almost an integral part of the C.N.R.
All the minister has told us is that he has had information from Canadian National Railways that they have had general discussions. Part of my reason for putting the question to the minister is to find out just how detailed the relationship has been between the C.N.R. and the Alberta government. I think in a sense we are entitled to know this, particularly because of the caution that has been expressed by the royal commission on transportation regarding the building of branch lines, and particularly because of our experience with the Gaspe railway, which is an indication that sometimes the railway building urge gets too strong.
On the other hand, Mr. Manning has a vision based upon resources that is quite impressive, and it would seem to me that the proposition was put to the C.N.R. that it should build the line. After all, it would be a natural and integral part of the C.N.R. system and it is Mr. Manning's hope that eventually the C.N.R. would buy the line. It seems to me that in these circumstances we deserve to hear from the minister what role,

if any, he as minister has played in this particular matter and what further information he can give as to why the C.N.R. apparently refused the invitation or opportunity to build the line on its own, probably because of lack of freight revenue-we need to know these details-but is apparently willing-or is it-to go ahead and build it under the general and rather hazy arrangements that Premier Manning has suggested.
If the resources are really there as the premier says, then it seems to me, given the general federal jurisdiction over railroading and the fact that the C.N.R. exists, that this is the kind of situation where some pretty strong leadership could come into play from the Minister of Transport in working with the provincial government and C.N.R. to develop something. Certainly the general belief amongst the people I have talked to in Alberta is that there are immense resources of timber, coal and so on to be exploited by this railway, and it seems to me that with regard to our railroading plans for the future we need something better than provincial premiers putting up trial balloons. We need some kind of policy from our federal Minister of Transport. It is for that reason I raised the question today, and in the three minutes he has I think he might honour us with more information than he has apparently been willing to give in answer to the two questions that have been put to him previously.

speechtext:
It is not
often I appear on this late show because I am an early to bed man. I was surprised that my question today, directed to the Minister of Public Works, did not go through the Speaker's gambit and I was asked to put it on the order paper. This I could not accept without taking advantage of the opportunity to debate it, because I was asking about something more than a mere local public works project. I was asking about a great national undertaking upon which recently more announcements have been made through the press than have been made by ministers of the government. I refer to the Prince Edward Island causeway, a multimillion dollar development project, as important as such great ventures as the South Saskatchewan dam, one of the national development projects of the government which for six or seven years I supported.
I have some comments and some inquiries, and I will give the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works an opportunity to expand on his answer. I am still concerned about government by press release,
12444	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion and progress from news item to news item on this very important matter. I have my files here on the Prince Edward Island causeway and they are quite thick. They are composed mostly of news items and very few parliamentary papers, because it is much easier, apparently, for reporters to extract information than it is for members representing the province of Prince Edward Island. I remember so well the days when the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill)

soon to be a senator I understand-was always asking for a report on this project. I wonder if he has become so enamoured of it that he is keeping it close to his chest, now he has resumed his place on the treasury benches.
I would say to the new minister, if he were here, that I hope he will be more forthcoming in giving information on this important project. Ever since Prince Edward Island entered confederation, transportation has been a vital question. I would commend, as I have done before, the example of the former prime minister when he stood in his place and, as prime minister, made a firm commitment on the matter. I was surprised also that the Minister of Transport, on his tour of Newfoundland, apparently did not make reference to this great project, so important to the whole Atlantic region. I am told that a statement was elicited from him on the way back by some very good reporter. I should have thought his pride would have caused him to expand and tell the people of Newfoundland how well they were doing in finishing up these projects. I would not say it was an afterthought, but it was significant that it had to be elicited from him by the press. I want to be co-operative. I want to be sanguine. I want to share Premier Shaw's delight, but I am still asking that some of the uncertainties be removed.
I hear on the radio that tenders are to be called. Then I hear that only the first one of the surveys has been completed and that phase 2 deals with the question of railways. How you can contemplate calling tenders when it has not been decided whether the causeway shall have rails or not, is something that passes my understanding. I want to know if the Minister of Public Works is sure that four to six weeks will complete this vast study. I want to know how he is going to go about this study. Will it be undertaken by his departmental officials?
Will interested and responsible bodies like the maritime transportation commission be presenting their opinions formally and officially to the government? Will the province
[Mr. Macquarrie.l

of P.E.I. be expressing its views? Will individuals be given a chance? Will Mr. Margison receive more information than he has got so far?
We do not want to surrender our railways in Prince Edward Island without a most attractive and realistic quid pro quo. I do not think press releases, no matter how frequently they come or how carefully they are worded, will do the trick. We need some proper information. We want clearcut plans. We want a chance for the people to know what is to be done.
It would be a profound change in our whole transportation pattern, indeed in our whole economic life, if we should lose the railway in Prince Edward Island. Our transportation needs are becoming more and more urgent. We want more information. There is need for a higher priority and a little more discussion about this great national undertaking in this house before the representatives of the people.

Mr. Speaker, the question I put to the Minister of Finance this afternoon, which I now put to the parliamentary secretary, is a very old one but it has been recently brought into focus.
When the government announced the decision to lower the eligible age for the old age security pension it indicated that it would take away the $500 extra income tax exemption during the years between 65 and 70 when people are drawing the old age security pension. There have been protests against this and I put the question to the Minister of Finance this afternoon in the following way:
In view of these protests would the minister consider as an alternative to taking away this $500 exemption between the ages of 65 and
16, 1965	12445
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion 70 the increasing of the income tax exemption level to $1,500 single and $3,000 married across the board?
As hon. members know, for a long time many people have felt that the present income tax exemption levels are not high enough. In theory they are supposed to indicate the amount of money a person should have to spend before taxation is applied. One thousand dollars for a single person is only $19.23 a week; $2,000 for a married person is only $38.46 a week. I think we all agree that this point is too soon to begin applying income tax. So I hope the Minister of Finance in preparing his budget will give consideration to a proposal different from the one announced by the Prime Minister on February 17 and that instead of taking away the extra $500 from those between 65 and 70 the government will decide to raise the levels across the board to $1,500 single and $3,000 married.
When I put my question this afternoon I added the important proviso that there would have to be an adjustment in tax rates when such a change was made so that the advantage would accrue mainly to those in the lower income brackets.
The Minister of Finance did not particularly like my question this afternoon. I gathered that he thought I was trying to get him to leak a budget secret. I know the Minister of Finance better than that and I hope he knows me better than that. I was not asking him to give a final answer and tell us what he proposes to do, but I did think it was proper to ask whether the government is considering this alternative approach to the problem and I hope I can have an answer to that question now from the parliamentary secretary.
